question: What process does Nickey Skarstad recommend for setting product vision and translating it into goals?
expected_points: Involve the team in shaping the strategy and gather context from organizational leaders.
Work top-down through the vision, mission, strategy, and objectives.
Make objectives concrete for the next three to six months.
evidence_quote: And all it is really is thinking about hitting those specific notes and thinking about them top down.

answer.summary: Skarstad recommends building vision with the team, then working down from long-term vision through mission and strategy to near-term OKRs that connect to execution. [S1, S2, S3, S4, S5]

sections.heading: Develop the vision collaboratively
sections.content: Do not create strategy alone and present it as a finished plan: involve the team so people help craft it and are more likely to buy in. For a visioning session, use a whiteboard tool such as FigJam, Miro, or MURAL, and brainstorm with a cross-functional group. Ask where the organization could be in 10 years and how the competitive landscape might change. Give participants room to think on a five-to-10-year horizon rather than focus on today's concerns. [S1, S2]

sections.heading: Translate vision down the strategy pyramid
sections.content: Start with the long-term vision and write down the ideal direction. Define the mission as how to bring that vision to life, then strategy as what needs to happen to execute it. Set objectives—using OKRs or another goal-setting model—to clarify what needs to be achieved in the next three to six months. [S3]

sections.heading: Connect goals to execution and review them regularly
sections.content: Good OKRs clearly articulate the strategy and make it actionable for the next period, so work at the feature or ticket level connects back to strategy. At Duolingo, Skarstad says quarterly OKR planning typically starts in the third month of the current quarter: assess progress and whether the commitments were right, then spend a few weeks deciding what will have the most impact next quarter and setting objectives and key results. Ideally, those goals plug into a longer-term plan; the process usually includes a leadership review. [S4, S5]

answer.summary: Nickey Skarstad recommends building the vision with the team, then translating it down a strategy “pyramid” into a shared set of near-term goals. Those goals should connect day-to-day work to the longer-term plan, with regular communication to keep the team aligned.

sections.heading: Set the vision collaboratively
sections.content: Don’t write strategy alone and announce it afterward: involve the team so people help shape the plan and are more likely to buy in. Run a broad, cross-functional visioning brainstorm—for example, using FigJam, Miro, or MURAL—and ask where the organization should be in 10 years and how the competitive landscape may change. Give people room to think beyond today’s concerns on a five-to-10-year horizon.

sections.heading: Translate vision into goals
sections.content: Work down a strategy pyramid: write down the long-term vision first; define the mission as how to bring it to life; set strategy by identifying what must happen to execute the vision; then use OKRs or another goal-setting model to specify the next three to six months. Good OKRs clearly articulate the strategy and bring it down to actionable work, so feature-level tasks connect back up to the strategy.

sections.heading: Plan and keep the goals grounded
sections.content: At Duolingo, quarterly OKR planning typically starts in the third month of the current quarter: review progress and commitments, then spend a few weeks deciding what would have the most impact next quarter and setting objectives and key results, followed by leadership review. She says OKRs aren’t right for every team, but a shared cross-functional goal framework helps translate strategy into what the team can act on now. After approval, recap leadership feedback and changes promptly, and revisit the strategy and how goals ladder up in weekly team meetings.

answer.summary: Skarstad recommends involving the team in a long-range vision exercise, then working down a strategy pyramid to turn the vision into near-term objectives and goals tied to execution. [S1, S2, S3, S4]

sections.heading: Develop the vision together
sections.content: Do not write strategy in isolation and present it as a fait accompli: involve the team so people help shape it and are more likely to buy in. For a visioning session, use a collaborative whiteboard such as FigJam, Miro, or MURAL and brainstorm questions like where the organization could be in 10 years and how the competitive landscape might change. Make it cross-functional by inviting people beyond the immediate team, and give them room to think on a five-to-ten-year horizon rather than focus on today’s constraints. [S1, S2]

sections.heading: Translate vision into goals from the top down
sections.content: Work down a pyramid: write the long-term vision first; define the mission as how to bring that vision to life; set strategy by identifying what must happen to execute it; then express objectives using OKRs or another goal-setting model. Goals should make the next three to six months’ priorities clear, and good OKRs articulate the strategy in actionable terms that connect all the way down to specific work, such as a feature or Jira ticket. [S3, S4]

sections.heading: Plan and align around the near-term goals
sections.content: At Duolingo, Skarstad describes quarterly OKRs: the process usually starts in the quarter’s third month with a review of progress and whether the team committed to the right things. The team then spends a few weeks shaping the next quarter’s work around what will have the most impact and advance the long-term strategy, setting objectives and key results, and getting leadership review. She cautions that OKRs are not right for every team, but recommends a shared goal-setting framework across functions. To keep goals connected to the strategy, she also describes communicating leadership feedback promptly and revisiting in weekly team meetings what the team is trying to achieve and how its goals ladder up. [S5, S6, S7, S8]
